text: What kind of leader does this team need right now, that may be different from the one they wanted last year?
evaluation: Phase fit. Founders, scalers, stabilisers, turnaround leaders are different shapes. Wrong shape costs years.

text: What kind of leader am I at my best, in two specific behaviours?
evaluation: Force concrete behaviours. 'Visionary' is not a behaviour. 'Holds weekly 1:1s I prepare for' is.

text: What kind of leader am I at my worst, in two specific behaviours?
evaluation: Worst-mode awareness predicts whether the team will weather the bad weeks.

text: What is the last decision I made that I would not make again, and why?
evaluation: Recent and specific. Watch for the lesson: process, judgement, missing information, or self-knowledge.

text: What is the last decision I made that surprised me by working, and what does that tell me?
evaluation: Surprise reveals model gaps. The lesson is the actual prize.

text: What is one decision I am avoiding making, and what is the cost per week of the delay?
evaluation: Force the cost number. Most avoided decisions are quietly expensive.

text: What is one decision I made too quickly, recently, and what would slowing down have cost?
evaluation: Both fast and slow have failure modes. Self-aware leaders know which one they fall to under stress.

text: What is the conversation I most need to have, with whom, by when?
evaluation: Three blanks. Fill all three.

text: What is the conversation I keep having that I should stop, with whom, and what's the alternative?
evaluation: Some recurring conversations are work; some are addiction. Tell them apart.

text: What kind of conflict do I avoid that costs the team most?
evaluation: Performance conversations, disagreements with peers, telling truth upward. The avoidance pattern is usually consistent.

text: What kind of conflict do I seek out that drains the team?
evaluation: Some leaders argue for sport, or to feel competent, or to avoid harder conversations.

text: What is one thing my team needs to hear from me that I have not said clearly?
evaluation: Often: 'I trust you on this.' 'I don't trust this on you yet.' 'You are not on track.' 'You are doing better than you think.'

text: What is one thing my team has been telling me that I have not let myself hear?
evaluation: Listen for the pattern across multiple voices. Solo dissent can be noise; chorus is signal.

text: What is one piece of feedback I gave that, on reflection, was about me, not them?
evaluation: Common: irritation projected as standards, anxiety projected as urgency, shame projected as 'high bar'.

text: What is one piece of feedback I withheld that, on reflection, was for me, not them?
evaluation: Withheld feedback is sometimes kindness, often cowardice, occasionally wisdom. Tell them apart.

text: What is one promotion I made that the team understood as fair, and what made it land that way?
evaluation: Process replicable: track record, communicated criteria, public reasoning. Catch what worked.

text: What is one promotion I made that the team did not understand as fair, and what would I do differently?
evaluation: Even when right, opacity is a cost. Reasoning out loud is part of the work.

text: What is one performance issue I let drift, and what did the drift teach the rest of the team?
evaluation: Drift teaches that the standard is the lowest tolerated behaviour. Address it sooner than feels comfortable.

text: What is one performance issue I addressed early, and what did that decisiveness teach the rest of the team?
evaluation: Counterpart. Decisiveness, done well, raises the floor for everyone.

text: What is one piece of trust I have with this team that I have not banked deliberately?
evaluation: Track record, shared crisis, kept promises. Knowing your trust capital lets you spend it wisely.

text: What is one piece of trust I have lost with this team that I have not earned back?
evaluation: Trust loss is specific. Name the moment, name the repair, do the repair, do not announce the repair.

text: What is the disagreement on this team that everyone is dancing around?
evaluation: Name it, neutrally, in a meeting. The relief alone is often worth the cost.

text: What is the agreement on this team that everyone is pretending exists, and doesn't?
evaluation: Phantom alignment. Cheaper to surface than to suffer.

text: What is one decision I have delegated in name but not in fact?
evaluation: Take-backs corrode trust. Either delegate fully or own openly.

text: What is one decision I have kept that I should have delegated?
evaluation: Common in technical leaders. The decision feels small to you and large to the person you would have grown by giving it.

text: What does this team look like in two years if I lead it well?
evaluation: Concrete picture. Composition, output, culture, what they would say about working here.

text: What does this team look like in two years if I lead it badly?
evaluation: Equally concrete. Failure scenarios discipline the present better than success scenarios.

text: What is one thing I do in meetings that I would coach a junior leader to stop doing?
evaluation: Coach yourself. The leader-pattern visible to others is rarely visible to self until externalised.

text: What is one thing I do in 1:1s that I would coach a junior leader to keep doing?
evaluation: Catalogue your strengths. They become coachable, repeatable, teachable.

text: What is the unspoken rule on this team that we should make spoken?
evaluation: Often: how to disagree, when to escalate, who decides what. Naming the rule reduces drama.

text: What is the spoken rule on this team that no one actually follows, including me?
evaluation: Either enforce it or strike it. Dead rules teach contempt for live ones.

text: What does loyalty to this team mean to me, in concrete behaviour?
evaluation: Force specifics. 'Defending in public, naming in private' is one shape; there are others.

text: What does loyalty to my own integrity mean to me, when it conflicts with loyalty to this team?
evaluation: Pre-decide the line. Hard to find under pressure if not pre-decided.

text: What is one thing I tolerate in a high performer that I would not tolerate in a low performer?
evaluation: Asymmetric tolerance corrodes faster than visible favouritism. Common and costly.

text: What is one thing I demand of a low performer that I do not demand of a high performer?
evaluation: Counterpart. Disproportionate demands disguised as 'expectations'.

text: What is one signal of burnout in myself I have learned to recognise?
evaluation: Sleep, irritability, withdrawal, loss of pleasure in craft. Knowing your tells lets you act early.

text: What is one signal of burnout in someone else I now spot earlier than I used to?
evaluation: Quality before energy. Withdrawal before complaint. Cynicism before quitting. Catch the early signal.

text: What is the conflict between two people on my team I have been calling 'a personality clash' that is actually a decision I have not made?
evaluation: Most 'personality clashes' are role overlaps, scope ambiguity, or unmade calls. Find the missing decision.

text: What is the conflict between two people on my team that is actually a personality clash, and how do I work with it?
evaluation: Some clashes are real. Structure around them: distance, separate scopes, named protocols. Don't insist on chemistry.

text: What is one criticism of me, recurring across roles, that may finally be the truth?
evaluation: Pattern recognition on self. If three managers, two peers, and your spouse have said the same thing, it's not them.

text: What is one strength of mine, recurring across roles, that I have learned to underplay?
evaluation: Underplayed strengths atrophy. Name them, claim them, use them.

text: What is the part of leadership I love that I rarely admit?
evaluation: Status, control, mentoring, building, decision-making, public credit. Naming the love stops it from running unchecked.

text: What is the part of leadership I dread that I rarely admit?
evaluation: Firing, public failure, performance reviews, being disliked. Naming the dread is half the work.

text: What is one thing I fired someone for that, on reflection, was a system failure, not theirs?
evaluation: Painful but useful. The lesson protects the next hire.

text: What is one thing I kept someone for, that I should have addressed sooner, and what did the delay cost?
evaluation: Counterpart. Delay's cost is paid in team morale, not just output.

text: What is the meeting on my calendar that I dread, and what would changing its shape cost?
evaluation: Dread is data. Change the cadence, attendees, format, or end the meeting outright. Small leadership move; large effect.

text: What is the meeting on my calendar that gives me energy, and how do I protect more of them?
evaluation: Energy-positive meetings often hold the actual creative work. Protect the cadence.

text: What is one thing my best peer leader does that I have been refusing to copy?
evaluation: Pride is expensive. Copying is the fastest growth lever in leadership.

text: What is one thing my worst peer leader does that I have started to do under pressure?
evaluation: Drift toward what you criticise. The criticism predicts the drift.

text: What is the principle I will not violate, even when it costs the project?
evaluation: Pre-decide. Hard to find a line in real time without one written down.

text: What is the principle I have already quietly violated, that I should restate aloud?
evaluation: Restating principles after a quiet breach is part of how cultures heal. Skipping the restatement is how they erode.

text: What is one piece of bad news I am sitting on that the team can handle better than I think?
evaluation: Adults handle bad news better than ambiguity. Withholding usually wounds more than telling.

text: What is one piece of bad news I am sharing too freely, that is shaping the team's mood beyond its size?
evaluation: Counterpart. Leaders who 'share everything' sometimes outsource their anxiety to the team.

text: What is one decision the team thinks I made that I actually inherited?
evaluation: Naming inheritances reduces unfair credit and unfair blame. Do it once, calmly.

text: What is one inheritance that I have made my own, that I should now retire?
evaluation: Old systems persist past their use. Identify, retire, replace, name the change.

text: What is the thing I am most often wrong about, that I have learned to flag in advance?
evaluation: Pre-warning your team about your reliable wrongness is a strong leadership move.

text: What is the thing I am most often right about, that I should be more confident asserting?
evaluation: Calibrated confidence is rare. Where your track record is strong, claim it.

text: What is one disagreement I had with my own boss this quarter that I handled well?
evaluation: Managing up is half the role. Catalogue what worked.

text: What is one disagreement I had with my own boss this quarter that I handled badly?
evaluation: And what would I do differently. Real growth lever.

text: What is the truth I am protecting my team from that they will need to hear within 90 days?
evaluation: Reorgs, runway, leadership change. Telling early gives people room to act; telling late corrodes trust.

text: What is the truth I am protecting myself from that I will need to hear within 90 days?
evaluation: Self-deception decays slower than reality. The 90-day clock helps.

text: What is one rule for hiring I have learned that I would only share with peers, not in public?
evaluation: Honest practitioner knowledge often differs from public discourse. Share carefully but honestly with peers.

text: What is one rule for firing I have learned that I would only share with peers, not in public?
evaluation: Same. Practitioner knowledge about exits is hard-won and rarely written down.

text: What is one moment in the last month when I led from fear, and what was the fear?
evaluation: Fear-led leadership is recognisable: rushed decisions, controlling behaviour, premature reorgs. Name the source.

text: What is one moment in the last month when I led from love, and what made that possible?
evaluation: Counterpart. Notice the conditions; reproduce them.

text: What is one habit of mine that scales with team size, and one that breaks?
evaluation: What works at five breaks at fifteen. Self-aware leaders re-engineer themselves at each phase.

text: What is one part of the team I have stopped paying attention to, that I should resume?
evaluation: Quiet competence often loses attention. Reverse the pattern.

text: What is one part of the team I am paying too much attention to, and what would happen if I stepped back?
evaluation: Often the part that matches our own former role. Stepping back is part of growing the team.

text: What is the next leader I need to develop on this team, and what would I trade for their growth?
evaluation: Force the trade. Growth costs scope, decisions, public credit. Real development requires real ceding.

text: What is the next leader on this team I am quietly blocking, and why?
evaluation: Blocking is rarely conscious. Threat, scarcity, paternalism, stuck mental models.

text: What is the unwritten contract I have with my team about how I will act in a crisis?
evaluation: Calm, present, honest, decisive. The contract is recognised before it is articulated.

text: What is the unwritten contract I have with my team about how I will act in good times?
evaluation: Generous, present, credit-giving, undefensive. Easier to honour in good times — and easier to violate.

text: What is one symbolic act I have done that was worth more than its cost?
evaluation: Stepping into a junior task, defending a peer publicly, walking out of a hostile room. Symbols are policy.

text: What is one symbolic act I should do soon, that I have been calculating around?
evaluation: Calculation is the wrong stance for symbolic acts. The cost of the act is usually less than the cost of withholding it.

text: What is the question I should be asking my team that I have been answering for them?
evaluation: Premature answers steal the team's growth. Hold the question open longer than feels comfortable.

text: What is the question my team is asking me that I have been deflecting?
evaluation: Deflection is visible. Answer or say honestly: 'I don't know yet, here's when I will.'

text: What is one thing I learned from a failure I have not yet generalised into a rule?
evaluation: Lessons unrules repeat themselves. Write the rule.

text: What is one rule I have been generalising from a single failure that may not deserve it?
evaluation: Counterpart. Single-instance rules over-correct. Re-examine periodically.

text: What is the ratio of repair to rupture I have been holding with this team, honestly?
evaluation: Repair is the work. Rupture is normal; consistent repair is the leadership signal.

text: What is one repair I owe a specific person, and when am I doing it?
evaluation: Force the calendar. Owed repairs decay in value if not paid promptly.

text: What is the team norm I will defend, even alone, and why?
evaluation: Pre-decide. The lonely defence often arrives without warning.

text: What is the team norm I have been defending out of habit that no longer serves us?
evaluation: Norms outlive their utility. Audit every quarter.

text: What is one thing my team would tell my boss about me, that I would be proud of?
evaluation: Imagined upward feedback. Often more telling than performance reviews.

text: What is one thing my team would tell my boss about me, that I would dread?
evaluation: Imagine the sentence. Then work to make it false.

text: What is one moment in this team's history I want us to remember together, and what kept it sacred?
evaluation: Shared memory is culture. Mark moments deliberately or they fade.

text: What is one moment in this team's history I want us to learn from but not return to, and what changed because of it?
evaluation: Learning without rumination. Mark the lesson; close the loop.

text: What is the rate of change I am asking this team to absorb, and is it sustainable?
evaluation: Change debt is real. Absorbing more than the team can metabolise produces churn that looks like attitude problems.

text: What is the rate of stability I am imposing on this team, and is it letting needed change in?
evaluation: Counterpart. Over-stability calcifies. Find the cadence.

text: What is one piece of authority I have that I rarely use, and what would using it cost?
evaluation: Hard veto, public stand, structural change. Authority unused atrophies and rusts.

text: What is one piece of authority I use too often, that the team has stopped responding to?
evaluation: Diluted authority. Use sparingly to keep it potent.

text: What is one moment when I should have apologised publicly and didn't?
evaluation: Public mistakes deserve public repair. Private apologies for public errors usually fall short.

text: What is one moment when I apologised publicly and it landed well, and why?
evaluation: Specific, brief, no excuse, named change. The format is replicable.

text: What is one assumption I am making about a difficult team member that may be unfair?
evaluation: Steelman them. Fairness costs little and recovers much.

text: What is one assumption I am making about a high performer that may be flattering them past the truth?
evaluation: Halo effect. Costly. Re-baseline periodically.

text: What is the kind of leader I want my children, or my younger self, to read about me being?
evaluation: Long horizon. The story of yourself you're writing in real time.

text: What is the kind of leader I am afraid I am quietly becoming?
evaluation: Drift is real. Naming the feared version is half the resistance to becoming it.

text: What is one decision this quarter that, if made well, will compound for years?
evaluation: Hires, structure, principles. Spend disproportionate care on these.

text: What is one decision this quarter that I am over-thinking, that probably matters less than I feel?
evaluation: Reversible decisions deserve fast moves. Save the careful thinking for the irreversible.

text: What is the version of myself, in two years, that I would feel relieved to have already become?
evaluation: Specificity helps. The relief reveals the cost of the present-day gap.

text: What is the next, smallest move toward that leader, that I can take this week?
evaluation: Closing. Small and dated. Action ends the cycle.
